one_liner: SIMD PRNG returning 128 bits per call via carry-less multiply; author's table puts it ahead of xoshiro256**, PCG64DXSM, MT19937.
what_it_does: A non-cryptographic generator with 32 bytes of state (two 128-bit vectors) that returns one 128-bit vector per call, with constant-time jumps of 2^64, 2^128 and 2^192 steps and a prev() step. The C version (c/culumi.c) is a single file of free functions (init, initState, next, nextRange, nextUInt4/nextInt4, nextDouble2, nextFloat4, nextBytes, jump64/128/192, prev) followed by a test main() you must strip before embedding. The C# version (csharp/Culumi.cs, about 3,000 lines) is a sealed class with a System.Random-style API plus extras (vector variants, Gaussian, exponential, GUID/ULID, BigInteger, Shuffle, GetItems, weighted choice, Split). Neither is a drop-in std:: engine: the C code returns __m128i, not a UniformRandomBitGenerator result.
how_it_is_fast: The state update is GF(2)-linear (an LFSR-type step): one PCLMULQDQ carry-less multiply of the low 64 bits by a constant, two XORs and a 64-bit lane swap, which is what makes the 2^256-1 period provable. The output scrambler is nonlinear and also cheap: a 64-bit-lane add of the two state halves, a pshufb byte shuffle, and another add. So each call yields 128 bits from a handful of SSE instructions. The helpers use the whole vector: four 32-bit or two 64-bit bounded integers per call (multiply-high with a rejection/carry fix-up, no division) and 4x float or 2x double conversions with FMA.
when_to_use: .NET 7/8 code that wants a faster, richer System.Random replacement: the author's BenchmarkDotNet table (i7-12700F) has Next() at 0.94 ns vs 1.62 ns, NextDouble() 1.08 vs 1.85 ns and Shuffle(char[16]) 19 vs 55 ns.
x86-64 C/C++ code that consumes random bits 128 at a time (bulk byte fills, SIMD Monte Carlo with 4x float or 2x double lanes) and wants a 32-byte state.
Parallel simulations that need many non-overlapping streams via constant-time jumps (2^128 streams of length 2^128 per the README).
Projects that want public-domain (CC0) code they can paste in without license tracking.
when_not_to_use: Anything security-sensitive: the README says the internal state was recovered from three consecutive 128-bit outputs with the Z3 solver in a few hours.
Portable C/C++: the C version uses x86 intrinsics and needs SSE4.1, PCLMUL and FMA; there is no ARM or scalar path in C (only the C# version has ARM and software fallbacks).

When you need a std::-compatible engine, a maintained library or independent numbers: 4 commits, all on 2023-05-25, no benchmark harness in the repo, and the ns/KiB table states no language, compiler or CPU.

If you just need fast scalar 64-bit outputs: the same table has SFC64 at 97.80 and xoroshiro128++ at 113.53 ns/KiB against Culumi's 58.68, a gap small enough that a portable, better-studied generator may be the better trade.

integration.form: source-drop (one C file with an embedded test main(); one C# file)
integration.dependencies: none (C: x86intrin.h or intrin.h, seeds from /dev/urandom or rand_s; C#: .NET base library only)
integration.min_toolchain: C: gcc/clang/MSVC with -msse4 -mpclmul -mfma (source comment); C#: README says .NET 7, the shipped Culumi.csproj targets net8.0
integration.platforms: C: x86-64 with SSE4.1 + PCLMULQDQ + FMA; C#: any .NET 7+ runtime, fast on x86 PCLMUL and ARM AES (PMULL), with a slow software carry-less multiply fallback elsewhere
integration.thread_safety: not documented; the state is a plain mutable struct/class with no locking, so use one instance per thread (jump() or C# Split() to separate streams)
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — the C# class mirrors System.Random method names (Next, NextDouble, NextBytes, Shuffle, GetItems) but does not derive from System.Random; the C code has no std::mt19937-style engine interface

gotchas: Correctness bug in the C port (found by reading the code; not run): the retry path of nextDouble2 and nextFloat4, taken when min + u*(max-min) rounds up to max, passes _mm_andnot_pd/_ps arguments in the wrong order (Intel's andnot(a,b) is ~a & b, while the C# original's Vector128.AndNot(a,b) is a & ~b), and nextDouble2's retry multiplies by min2 where max2 belongs. A lane that already succeeded is zeroed and the retried lane gets garbage bits. The retry is rare for ranges near zero but common for narrow ranges at large magnitude (about 6% of draws per lane for [1e15, 1e15+1), derived). The C# version is correct.
nextBytes stores through an __m128i* cast of the caller's byte buffer, which compilers may emit as aligned stores, so pass a 16-byte-aligned buffer.

In C, next() is declared non-static 'inline' (DLLEXPORT inline), which under C99 inline rules can fail to link at -O0, and the exported names (init, next, prev, jump64) are generic enough to collide; rename or make them static inline when vendoring.
initState() calls exit(-1) on an all-zero seed, and init() falls back to time()/clock() seeding, which the source comment says lacks entropy, if /dev/urandom cannot be read.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Culumi over the same author's scalar Shioi and Seiran when you can rely on x86 PCLMUL (or .NET) and consume 128-bit vectors. For raw bulk throughput SHISHUA is the stronger sibling (its own README claims 52.93 GB/s, about 19 ns/KiB derived, against Culumi's 58.68 ns/KiB), and SIMD xoshiro ports such as simdrng suit you better if you want a well-analysed generator with C++ engine semantics.
verified_claims_summary: The README's comparison table lists Culumi at 58.68 ns per KiB against xoshiro256** 137.79, PCG64DXSM 308.30 and MT19937_32 547.58 (about 2.3x, 5.3x and 9.3x, derived from page data). It names no language, compiler, flags or CPU and ships no harness; its baseline links point at .NET, Java and Unity generators, SFMT comes out slower than MT, and Shishua is listed at 220.97 ns/KiB, far below SHISHUA's own figures, so the baselines look like scalar managed ports, not std::mt19937 or SIMD code. A separate BenchmarkDotNet run (.NET 8 preview, RyuJIT AVX2, i7-12700F, Windows 11) puts Culumi's Next() at 0.937 ns against System.Random's 1.619 ns (1.73x); its benchmark code is not published either.
status_note: Abandoned (4 commits, all on 2023-05-25; 4 stars, no issues filed) but CC0 and one file per language, so it is easy to vendor; prefer the C# file, or fix the C retry bug before using the C range helpers.
